description: Team Star Platinum brings together Ukrainian analysts, engineers, and a physicist, combining expertise in physics, Data Science, Python, web development, and UI/UX design. For the NASA Space Apps Challenge, we are building a pipeline to process SPHEREx spectral and astrometric data to search for Planet X. We focus on developing an intuitive web interface delivering the analytical depth required by professional scientists alongside accessible, clear visualizations for aspiring researchers.
summary:
Star Platinum is an open web tool that turns NASA’s public all-sky infrared survey SPHEREx (0.75–5.0 µm) into a convenient blink comparator. The user enters an object name or coordinates and sees images of that region of the sky in four modes: Frames, Stacks, Blink and Diff. With one click, you can get a source’s spectrum and check it against the SIMBAD and Gaia catalogues.
SPHEREx data (over 1.6 million frames) is too large to work with directly, and moving or variable objects only become visible when images from different epochs are compared. This is exactly what the NASA Space Apps challenge “Planet X and SPHEREx” requires: finding moving bodies in this data. We make this comparison accessible without specialist skills.
The tool is available to everyone, from schoolchildren to researchers, and lays the groundwork for searching for moving bodies, including Planet X candidates. We are honest about the limits: the Planet X search is currently visual, and both the saturation of bright stars and the SPHEREx pixel size limit accuracy. For validation, we reproduced known phenomena: the Barnard’s Star shift matched the Gaia DR3 prediction, and Paα and PAH 3.3 µm lines were detected in the Orion Nebula.
details:
Star Platinum is an open web tool that uses NASA’s public all-sky infrared survey SPHEREx (0.75–5.0 µm) to work with astronomical data. It shows what has changed or moved in one area of the sky between images taken several months apart.

We built an index of over 1.6 million SPHEREx frames in a PostgreSQL database. When a user enters an object name or coordinates, the system finds all images of that location and downloads only the needed fragments from NASA’s public AWS storage, rather than whole large files. These fragments are aligned to a common grid, the background glow is removed, and images from a single visit are stacked into one clear image.

The sky region can be set by object name, coordinates, or on an interactive sphere. The following modes are available for the selected region:

  • Frames – viewing individual images;
  • Stacks – stacked images;
  • Blink – rapid switching between images so that moving and variable objects “jump” or flicker;
  • Diff – a difference image where objects that changed brightness appear as light and dark spots.

Clicking on a source shows its spectrum in the 0.75–5 µm range, computed on the fly. We take known stars and objects from the SIMBAD and Gaia catalogues and shift them to the image date, accounting for their proper motion, in order to isolate the unknown.

Researchers can set up ideal viewing conditions: change the field size and the image processing, from brightening fainter stars to bringing out detail in bright ones. A system was built for quickly finding a specific frame by detector and wavelength. Additional settings are available for experienced users: colour range, contrast, background removal (sky median or NASA’s zodiacal light model), stacking methods (minmax, sigma, mean), stacking window (one visit, one day, or custom dates), and comparison of two methods. In the area analytics section, you can view general data about the region.

Advantages of the tool:

  • easy updating with new SPHEREx data;
  • intuitive functionality that requires no special skills;
  • for beginners: name search with autocomplete, tooltips for the controls, the mascot helper Platy, a sky sphere for choosing a region, and a mobile interface;
  • the view state is encoded in the URL, so any view can be saved as a link and embedded in other sites.

Validation. We verified that the method works on phenomena already known to science. These are reproductions of known results, not new discoveries:

  • Barnard’s Star: the measured shift of 10.3″ over 0.99 years matches the Gaia DR3 prediction (10.29″);
  • Epsilon Indi B agreed with Gaia within 2.5σ;
  • RW Aur (a known variable star): brightness decreased by 46%;
  • Orion Nebula: the Paα line (24σ) and PAH 3.3 µm (29σ) were detected.

Goal of the project: to make searching for moving and variable objects in SPHEREx data accessible to everyone, from schoolchildren to researchers, and to lay the groundwork for finding unseen bodies near the Solar System, including Planet X candidates. We honestly state the limitations: the Planet X search is currently visual, and both the saturation of bright stars and the SPHEREx pixel size limit accuracy.

Future plans. Star Platinum will become not only a tool but also a community platform: we plan articles and live discussion in the “Blog” section. We also plan:

  • more viewing settings, based on what users request most often;
  • personal accounts;
  • data export;
  • the ability to report objects found;
  • automated search for moving objects: deep learning models for motion analysis.

Technologies used:

  • Programming languages: Python 3.12, JavaScript (ES modules, no build step), HTML/CSS.
  • Data processing: Astropy and NumPy (FITS/WCS, computation); boto3 (HTTP byte ranges) for downloading fragments from the public SPHEREx archive on AWS S3.
  • Database: PostgreSQL 16 (via psycopg 3) for fast frame lookup.
  • Server: REST API built on FastAPI and Uvicorn.
  • Client: responsive interface in plain HTML/CSS and JavaScript, working in a browser on a computer, tablet or smartphone.
  • Deployment and quality: Docker, Docker Compose, Caddy (automatic HTTPS), pytest (82 unit tests), GitHub Actions for CI/CD.
  • Hardware: no special equipment is needed for the user, only a browser. The server side is deployed on a Hetzner server (https://www.hetzner.com/).
